title: What to Do When Someone Dies in Laos: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: What to Do When Someone Dies in Laos: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step bereavement checklist for Laos: medical death certification, civil death registration, funeral and repatriation permits, survivor benefits, and estate succession.
introHtml: When a citizen of the Lao People's Democratic Republic dies in Laos, key procedures involve prompt village-level reporting or medical certification, District civil registration within 30 days alongside household census updates, social security claims with the Lao Social Security Organization, and estate settlement under the 2018 Civil Code (in force since May 2020). Because Lao domestic ministries publish limited English-language procedural portals online and domestic web pages frequently run solely in Lao or with restricted accessibility, this checklist synthesizes official consolidated translations from the Lao Official Gazette, Lao Social Security Organization (LSSO), Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) legal portal, ILO NATLEX, UNESCAP CRVS, Lao News Agency, and accredited consular notices [1][2][4][8][9].

steps.title: Immediate medical certification and village or police reporting
steps.html:
• Hospital or health-facility death: The attending medical facility issues the official medical certificate of death required to proceed with local clearance and district registration [8][10].
  • Death at home or unexpected death: For a natural death at home, notify the Village Chief (Nai Ban) promptly (typically within 24 to 48 hours; UNESCAP CRVS documents a 5-day mandate for Village Chiefs to issue the local death notification form) [8][10][11].
  • Sudden, accidental, or suspicious death: Contact local police immediately so public security and health officials can examine the circumstances, complete forensic investigation where needed, and issue body-release clearance prior to burial or cremation [10][11].

steps.title: Civil death registration and household census updates
steps.html:
• Thirty-day statutory registration window: Under the amended Law on Family Registration framework tracked by UNESCAP CRVS and consular reciprocity guidance, register the death within 30 days at the District Office of Home Affairs (or designated District civil registration office) having jurisdiction over the deceased's residence or place of death [8][11].
  • Required civil registration documents: Present the medical death certificate or Village Chief death notification, the deceased's Lao National ID card, the household Family Census Book (Peum Sum Ma No Kua / electronic census certificate records now transitioning under Ministry of Public Security modernization reported by Lao News Agency (KPL)), and the informant's identity card [8][9][11].
  • Certified extracts and historical record note: Obtain multiple official Death Certificates (Bai Yang Yeun Kan Tai) at registration; note that U.S. reciprocity records observe that pre-1975 Lao civil records are often unavailable if historical reconstruction is ever needed [11].

steps.title: Burial, cremation, repatriation, and consular legalization
steps.html:
• Burial and cremation clearance: Religious and temple funeral rites or burial require prior medical or Village Chief death clearance and police authorization where the death occurred outside hospital care [10].
  • International transport of remains or ashes: Repatriating remains abroad requires the official Death Certificate, embalming or cremation certificate, medical non-infectious disease clearance, passport cancellation, and airline/customs permits [10][11].
  • Lao PDR is not an Apostille Convention party: As listed on the Hague Conference on Private International Law status table, Lao PDR is not a Contracting Party to the 1961 Hague Apostille Convention; documents intended for foreign jurisdictions must be translated, notarized by the Lao Notary Office, authenticated by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Lao PDR in Vientiane, and legalized by the destination embassy or consulate [10][11][12].

steps.title: Social security (LSSO) funeral and survivor benefits
steps.html:
• Funeral allowance under Lao Social Security Law: Under the Law on Social Security (Law No. 34/NA of 26 July 2013, indexed on ILO NATLEX, and Amended Law No. 54/NA of 27 June 2018), Lao Social Security Organization (LSSO) provides a one-time funeral allowance equal to 15 months of insured salary upon the death of an insured contributor, pensioner, or invalidity beneficiary (with 6 months on spouse death and 3 months on child death) [4][5][6][7].
  • Survivor / family benefit claims: Lao Social Security Organization (LSSO) pays family survivor allowances scaled by contribution duration (starting at 15 months for 3 to 12 months of contributions and increasing up to 24 months for long-term contributors) alongside ongoing survivor entitlements where qualifying criteria are satisfied [5][6].
  • Cancel identity records and freeze accounts: Update the household registry at District Public Security offices, cancel the deceased's passport and identity card, and present the official Death Certificate to banks and employers [9][11].

steps.title: Estate administration under the 2018 Civil Code
steps.html:
• Wills and statutory inheritance: Under the Civil Code of the Lao PDR (Law No. 55/NA of 6 December 2018, effective 27 May 2020, hosted by Lao Official Gazette and Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) Legal Portal), Part VIII unifies Laos's prior family and inheritance statutes, regulating written, notarized, and oral emergency wills alongside statutory heir classes and protected shares [1][2][3].
  • Notarized estate settlement and land titles: Heirs coordinate inheritance division certificates before the State Notary Office or District/Provincial People's Court if contested, and transfer Land Use Rights Certificates (Bai Ta Din) at the District Natural Resources and Environment Office [1][2].
  • Debts, tax, and cross-border assets: Estate assets pay funeral expenses and verified debts before distribution; foreign estate documents require translation and consular legalization before Lao courts or land offices will accept them [1][11].
